sections.heading: Read the Pitchfork Wind-Up
paragraphs: Haybots telegraph before the poke lands. Backpedal through the wind-up instead of trading a full swing in place, then re-engage once the arm resets. Crowded ruins punish players who stand still to finish a last hammer hit.
bullets: Pull one Haybot out of a ruin doorway before fighting the group.
Use a short water interruption when two wind-ups overlap.
Park fragile vehicles outside the pitchfork arc.

sections.heading: Scrap Metal First, Bonus Drops Second
paragraphs: Every Haybot pays Scrap Metal. Circuit Boards and Component Kits are bonus-table outcomes—expect empty rolls half the time and plan Circuit Board farming around Totebots when you need guaranteed boards.

sections.heading: Durability Beats Wishful Wood Walls
paragraphs: Haybot melee uses a break-chance table, not a simple HP bar on blocks. Soft scrap-wood shells fail often; higher durability tiers drop the break chance sharply, and durability 8+ is immune to Haybot destruction.
steps: Upgrade farm-facing walls before expanding crop value.
Leave a kite lane in front of the wall so you are not pinned against it.
Repair after raids instead of assuming unbroken panels mean the design worked.

sections.heading: When Haybots Share the Field With Worse Targets
paragraphs: On raid nights and ruin clears, Haybots are the volume problem, not always the priority kill. Clear explosive Totebots and Tapebots first when those silhouettes appear, then finish Haybots once the lane is controllable.

sections.heading: Ammo Math Versus Hammer Risk
paragraphs: A Spudgun at 28 damage needs about four hits for a 100 HP Haybot. That is cheap compared with Farmbot fights, so spend potatoes freely when a pitchfork group threatens a crop row or a loaded hauler.

properties.value: Walk-over and melee break chances on low durability

properties.value: Range first; light vehicles last

tables.note: The Warehouse Key is the progression-critical drop. Component Kits and Circuit Boards layer on top of the guaranteed key.

tables.note: Spud Shotgun has falloff at long range. Close-range full hits are the most ammo-efficient Farmbot kill.

tables.note: Farmbots can destroy low-durability blocks simply by walking over them. Metal Block 3 is the practical defense ceiling.

sections.heading: Budget Potatoes Before You Pull
paragraphs: Farmbot is an ammunition problem as much as an aiming problem. Spudgun needs about 54 shots at 28 damage; Shotgun needs roughly 24 full close-range hits; Spudling needs about 75 chunks. Count the potatoes on the vehicle before the pull, and keep a separate escape reserve.
bullets: Prefer Spud Shotgun only when you can stay in full-damage range.
Do not empty the base defense chest into one Warehouse run.
Mountable Spudguns share the 28-damage profile—plan container capacity accordingly.

sections.heading: Pesticide Is Why Standing Still Fails
paragraphs: Kick and swipe hurt, but the pesticide DoT punishes players who plant themselves behind a thin wall and trade hits. Keep moving laterally, break line of spray when possible, and heal between engagements instead of finishing the fight on empty stamina and food.

sections.heading: Warehouse Key Is the Real Loot
paragraphs: Every Farmbot drops a Warehouse Key. Component Kits and Circuit Boards are valuable extras, but the key unlocks the Warehouse progression loop. Secure the key immediately after the kill—do not leave it on the ground while looting secondary bots.

sections.heading: Metal Block 3 Is the Practical Shell
paragraphs: Farmbots destroy soft shells by walking and melee. Durability 1–3 breaks every time; higher tiers improve odds, but Metal Block 3 is the community practical ceiling for serious Farmbot-facing walls. Wood vanity walls belong behind that shell, not in front of it.
steps: Build a kill lane that keeps the Farmbot off crop soil.
Leave a kite path that does not dead-end into your own vehicle.
Recover the key and ammo before repairing cosmetic damage.

sections.heading: Disengage Rules That Save Vehicles
paragraphs: A light buggy dies to one bad corner. If the Farmbot reaches the hauler, abandon the DPS race and extract the vehicle first. A failed Farmbot fight with a lost cargo truck costs more than waiting for another encounter with a full potato loadout.

name: Totebot
description: The small 40 HP melee bot that always drops a Circuit Board—fast, swarm-prone, and the baseline for reading every Totebot color variant that shares its silhouette.

facts.value: Color and explosive variants share the body language

properties.value: Normal

sections.heading: Circuit Boards on Every Kill
paragraphs: Totebots are the dependable Circuit Board source in early Survival. Unlike Haybot bonus rolls, the board is guaranteed—clear packs deliberately when you need Craftbot and logic parts, then leave the area before another wave arrives.

sections.heading: Split the Pack Before You Swing
paragraphs: Forty health dies quickly, but fifteen damage per hit stacks when three Totebots pin you against a crop row or vehicle bumper. Strafe through openings, drop one body, then reset distance. Never back into a dead-end farm alley.
bullets: Pull packs off soil beds into open dirt or roadway.
Hammer the nearest bot only after the second cannot reach you in the same beat.
Loot Circuit Boards after the last idle sound stops.

sections.heading: Silhouette Literacy for Color Variants
paragraphs: 1.0 expands Totebot colors and behaviors. Treat unfamiliar paint as an unknown damage profile until confirmed. The Red Explosive Totebot keeps the small frame but changes the entire priority order—identify it before committing hammer range.

sections.heading: Raid Nights Versus Ruin Runs
paragraphs: On exploration routes, Totebots are loot opportunities. On raid nights, they are crop-pressure tools. The same bot asks for different spacing: ruins favor aggressive clears; farms favor funneling packs into a prepared lane away from seedlings.
steps: Mark a raid funnel that does not cross potato ammo chests.
Keep one Spudgun magazine for packs that break the funnel.
Store Circuit Boards away from the approach wall so you are not tempted to loot mid-fight.

sections.heading: Compare the Baseline Table
paragraphs: Totebot sits at the bottom of the Normal combat comparison: lowest health, lowest single-hit damage, highest drop reliability for Circuit Boards. Use that baseline to judge when a fight has escalated into Haybot or Tapebot territory.

name: Tapebot
description: The ranged bot family covering standard blue tape, red explosive shots, green bubble-plastic fire, and yellow slowing ink across Warehouses, Growlabs, and raids.

properties.value: Accurate ranged pressure

tables.note: Blue Tapebots deal 55 damage; Red Tapebots deal 62. Drop rates are shared on the documented loot table.

sections.heading: Peek One Angle, Not the Whole Room
paragraphs: Tapebots punish full doorway exposures. Slice the room: clear the visible shooter, return to hard cover, then open the next angle. Crossing the center for a Battery on the floor is how Warehouse runs end early.
bullets: Bring a real potato reserve—misses cost more than Totebot fights.
Check elevated and side balconies before looting desks.
Never use the cargo truck as disposable cover inside the building.

sections.heading: Blue Versus Red Projectile Weight
paragraphs: Both color lines sit at 40 HP, so time-to-kill is similar with a Spudgun. The difference is incoming damage: Blue at 55 and Red at 62 make mistakes lethal faster. Treat Red as the stricter cover check when both are present.

sections.heading: Battery Farming With Empty-Roll Patience
paragraphs: Roughly half of Tapebot kills return nothing on the documented table. Batteries appear about 35.7% of the time and Component Kits about 14.3%. Plan electrical crafting around multiple Warehouse clears, not a single lucky kill.

sections.heading: Interior Lighting and Sound Discipline
paragraphs: Dark Warehouse corridors hide muzzle flashes until you are already committed. Use Glowsticks or vehicle lights from behind cover, listen for the tape-fire cue, and do not sprint past uncleared corners while overloaded with loot.
steps: Light the next intersection from cover.
Eliminate the Tapebot before picking up floor loot.
Stage Batteries in a hallway chest before the next floor.

sections.heading: When Raids Bring Tapebots to the Farm
paragraphs: High plant-value farms can invite ranged bots into open fields. Soft wood fences fail as cover against 55–62 damage shots. Add metal or concrete peek panels on the raid approach and fight from those, not from crop soil.

sections.heading: Green and Yellow Tapebots Change the Room
paragraphs: Green Tapebots use weaponized bubble plastic and are most dangerous in groups that fill a corridor with overlapping fire. Yellow Tapebots use sorting ink that both damages and slows, turning an exposed retreat into a failed retreat. Growlab cover needs multiple exits so a slowing hit does not trap the player behind one corner.
bullets: Blue: treat every exposed angle as a high-damage shot lane.
Red: leave the impact area before the explosive projectile lands.
Green: avoid standing where several bubble paths overlap.
Yellow: preserve extra retreat distance before the slowing ink connects.

name: Red Explosive Totebot
description: A volatile 40 HP Totebot variant that ignites its payload, rushes the target, explodes near players or creations, and has no normal loot reward.
imageAlt: Red Explosive Totebot from Scrap Mechanic 1.0

facts.label: Threat
facts.value: Explosive pressure near players and creations

facts.label: Fight rule
facts.value: Range and distance over hammer trades

facts.label: Farm risk
facts.value: High near fuel, crops, and packed vehicles

properties.label: Identification
properties.value: Red explosive silhouette among Totebot packs

properties.label: Priority rank
properties.value: Above standard Totebots and most Haybots in mixed fights

properties.label: Safe distance
properties.value: Create space before finishing other melee bots

properties.label: Drop route
properties.value: No Circuit Board or material reward

sections.heading: Call It Out Before the Pack Closes
paragraphs: In multiplayer, the first player who sees red explosive paint should name the target. Split fire across random Totebots while an explosive closes distance is the common failure mode. One focused Spudgun burst beats three hammer players overlapping in blast range.

sections.heading: Distance Is the Mitigation
paragraphs: Forty health disappears quickly at range, but the detonation can still destroy the things around the bot. Back into open ground, keep a lateral escape path, and do not finish the fight pressed against gasoline, seed chests, or a loaded hauler.
bullets: Move fuel and crop storage off the usual raid funnel.
Avoid doorways that trap blast radius against the player.
Keep the final shot away from the vehicle and storage line.

sections.heading: Mixed Pack Ordering
paragraphs: Standard Totebots are Circuit Board farm; Red Explosive Totebots are incident prevention. Kill order: explosive first, Tapebots if present, then remaining melee. Haybots can wait if the explosive is still mobile.
steps: Identify paint and behavior at engagement start.
Spend potatoes on the explosive before hammering the pack.
Resume normal Totebot looting only after the blast threat is gone.

sections.heading: Vehicles and Soft Creations
paragraphs: Light frames and scrap-wood attachments take catastrophic damage from close detonations. Park creations outside the expected fight radius, or accept that a win can still cost a rebuild if the bot dies on top of the bumper.

sections.heading: There Is No Loot Reason to Close Distance
paragraphs: Its normal death table is empty. Unlike a Green Totebot, the red explosive variant is not a Circuit Board farm, so there is no reason to rush into the blast area to secure a drop.

name: Minerbot
description: A 140 HP flying underground threat that rains rocks on mining crews, crashes when shot down, and drops a Component Kit with tier-matched ore nuggets.

facts.label: Ore drop
facts.value: Nuggets matched to the spawn tier

properties.label: Vertical threat
properties.value: Attacks from above the dig face

properties.label: Crash hazard

properties.label: Spudgun estimate

sections.heading: Scan the Ceiling Before the Bore
paragraphs: A Plasma Drill run that only watches the rock face will miss Minerbots overhead. Pause at each chamber expansion, look up, and clear airspace before extending another long bore. Tunnel vision is the real damage multiplier.
bullets: Carry a Spudgun underground even on pure mining days.
Avoid ceilings that block player view while bots still fit above.
Stage cargo behind the active dig, not under the flight path.

sections.heading: Rock Shower Spacing
paragraphs: When rocks start falling, lateral movement beats standing under the drill arm. Break contact with the machine briefly, engage the Minerbot, then resume excavation. Operators who clutch the controls through the shower lose both health and the vehicle.

sections.heading: Plan the Crash Zone
paragraphs: Shot-down Minerbots fall. Finish them over empty floor or back toward already-cleared stone—not over the drill head, fuel, or a parked ore sled. If the only angle is above cargo, relocate the cargo first.
steps: Identify a clear crash pocket.
Draw the Minerbot over that pocket with movement.
Shoot it down and confirm the wreck before restarting the drill.

sections.heading: Light the Vertical Column
paragraphs: Dark shafts hide flying outlines until the first rock hits. Place lights that illuminate upward volume, not only the floor path. Sound cues plus a lit column turn Minerbots into readable targets instead of surprise damage.

sections.heading: Five Spudgun Hits Set the Ammo Floor
paragraphs: At 140 HP, five 28-damage Spudgun hits remove the normal health bar if every shot lands. Carry more than that per encounter: misses, additional underground bots, and the return route all compete for the same Potato reserve.

sections.heading: Corn In, Milk Out
paragraphs: The Woc loop is simple: present Corn, wait for the eat interaction, collect Woc Milk. Carry only the Corn you intend to feed so you do not spill seed-chest inventory into the animal area by mistake.

sections.heading: Build a Calm Feeding Pocket
paragraphs: Wocs need space more than architecture. A quiet meadow edge or modest pen beats a maze of logic gates. Keep spinning bearings, vehicle wheels, and active thrusters away from the feeding spot so the animal is not trapped or clipped by machinery.
bullets: Leave gate clearance wide enough for the Woc and the player.
Do not park the hauler inside the pen overnight.
Collect Milk before starting a nearby raid defense.

sections.heading: Route Corn Without Mixing Seed Lines
paragraphs: Corn for Wocs competes with other farm logistics only if storage is messy. Label a Corn crate for animal feed and keep tomato, potato, and high-value seeds elsewhere. Automation that dumps all produce into one vacuum line will starve the Milk loop.
steps: Stage Corn beside the pen, not beside the Spudgun ammo chest.
Feed, collect Milk, then restock Corn from the labeled crate.
Move Milk to the cooking / quest storage area in one trip.

sections.heading: Quest Context Without Overbuilding
paragraphs: Farmer-line quests featuring Wocs reward a working feed loop, not a decorative zoo. Complete the Milk interaction reliably before expanding pens into a theme park that blocks crop watering paths.

sections.heading: Protect the Animal From Raid Spillover
paragraphs: Hostile bots do not care that a Woc is passive. Place pens behind the defense line or far enough from the raid radius that pitchfork swings and Tapebot shots do not turn a Milk stop into a rebuild. Reposition after the first raid that clips the fence.

sections.heading: Cardboard Is the Currency
paragraphs: Glowbs convert Cardboard Blocks into Glow. Bring a deliberate cardboard stack—not your entire building inventory—and feed where the creature can path without clipping into terrain or a parked hull.

sections.heading: Feed in Reachable Water, Not a Trap Cove
paragraphs: Drop cardboard where the Glowb can approach freely. Narrow rock pockets and vehicle wedges pin the creature and waste cardboard. After it eats enough, collect Glow immediately so waves or current do not hide the product.
bullets: Clear Totebots or other hostiles before the feed run.
Feed piece by piece until timing and pathing are obvious.
Mark the exit from dark caves before you commit a large stack.

sections.heading: Glow Belongs With Battery Ingredients
paragraphs: Treat Glow as an electrical/chemical input, not a decorative dump item. Store it beside Battery ingredients and Chemicals so Craftbot sessions do not stall while you dig through building crates.
steps: Collect Glow into a dedicated chest or vehicle crate.
Return to base before starting Battery crafts.
Restock Cardboard only after Glow is secured.

sections.heading: Dark-Area Navigation
paragraphs: Many Glowb sightings sit in low-light terrain. Carry Glowsticks or vehicle lights, keep a return bearing, and do not block the creature with a boat or drill while interacting. Getting lost after a successful feed wastes the trip.

sections.heading: Quest Feed Versus Production Feed
paragraphs: A one-time quest ask needs a small cardboard delivery. Ongoing Battery production needs a renewable cardboard source and a repeatable water stop. Do not overbuild a permanent pen until you know you need Glow every session.

sections.heading: Read the Crate Before You Chase
paragraphs: Seedbot is not a random mixed-seed container. Its saved seed type controls both the visible head crate and every seed it releases. Identify the crop first; chasing a Tomato carrier when the field needs Broccoli only creates the wrong inventory.
bullets: Use color and crate art to identify the crop before the first hit.
Clear nearby hostile bots so the Seedbot does not flee through a second fight.
Leave an empty inventory slot for the matching seed stack.

sections.heading: Why One Huge Hit Can Release Several Seeds
paragraphs: The 100 HP bar is split into five health segments. Damage releases a matching seed for every segment crossed, so a strong hit can trigger more than one release at once. The destroyed state then uses a separate matching bundle.

sections.heading: Seedbot Is a Seed Source, Not Farm Automation
paragraphs: After collecting seeds, the farm still needs Soil, water, growth time, and harvesting. Use a Vacuum Pump build for repeatable planting or collection and keep its seed chest separate from the produce chest.
steps: Move the matching seeds into a labeled planting chest.
Keep harvested crops in a different container.
Check the Raid Calculator before turning the new seeds into a larger field.

sections.heading: Neutral Does Not Mean Indestructible
paragraphs: Seedbot has no attack state and tries to escape, but player attacks, vehicle collisions, crushing, and explosions can damage it. Decide whether the required seed supply justifies destroying it; do not mistake its fleeing behavior for an incoming raid.

sections.heading: Rapid Fire Wastes Hits
paragraphs: Lootbot accepts one point of damage, starts a 40-tick cooldown, and ignores further damage until that window ends. Spamming shots can spend ammunition without advancing the fourteen-point sequence or producing another reward.
bullets: Land one hit, watch the drop, then time the next hit.
Use open terrain so the fleeing route stays visible.
Collect rewards without stepping directly into the bot's escape line.

sections.heading: Hit Rewards and Death Rewards Are Different
paragraphs: The regular hit pool mixes useful materials, crops, energy items, and junk. The default raid death reward is a separate choice between ten Broccoli and ten Pineapples. Special encounters can replace that final reward with an outfit-package table.

sections.heading: Use the Crop Result Correctly
paragraphs: Lootbot releases produce, not seeds. A Tomato reward can feed Cookbot recipes or storage, but it does not replace a Tomato Seedbot when the objective is to expand the planting stock.
steps: Move produce into the harvest or Cookbot chest.
Move Component Kits, Batteries, and Gasoline into workshop storage.
Keep any Seedbot drops in a separate planting chest.

sections.heading: Why Lootbot Counts as Neutral
paragraphs: Its movement logic looks for nearby players and flees; it does not create a melee or ranged attack. The chase is an optional resource decision, not a defensive emergency, so clear hostile bots before spending time on the reward sequence.

sections.heading: Ten HP Does Not Mean Harmless
paragraphs: Cablebot dies quickly once targeted, but its value comes from reaching the machine rather than winning a long duel. It searches nearby bodies and shapes, prefers valid destructible targets, and can attack the working parts a mining vehicle needs to leave the area.

sections.heading: Clay Is Not a Permanent Lockout
paragraphs: Cablebot can request voxel destruction while moving toward a target. A quick terrain plug can buy time, but it should not be the only protection around a parked vehicle, storage node, or exposed power train.
bullets: Keep the driver path clear enough to move immediately.
Armor the working-part mounts rather than only the decorative body.
Clear nearby Cablebots before opening the service side.

sections.heading: Cable Roll Farming Is a One-in-Four Route
paragraphs: The normal death roll gives one Cable Roll at 25% and nothing at 75%. Plan several encounters for a required cable count instead of treating each kill as a guaranteed material pickup.

sections.heading: Build Response for Underground Vehicles
paragraphs: A mining vehicle needs protected mounts, visible service access, and an exit path more than a fully enclosed cosmetic shell. Put irreplaceable components behind the first layer and keep low-value armor easy to replace after a bite or dig-in.

sections.heading: Seeker Bot and Scannerbot Refer to the Same Search
paragraphs: Players commonly call this roaming missile encounter the Seeker Bot. The current unit and manager names use Scannerbot. Keeping both names on the page helps identify the same threat without inventing a separate enemy.

sections.heading: Why the Health-Bar Strategy Fails
paragraphs: Projectile and melee impacts play a no-progress response, while explosion, collision, and crush handlers do not apply damage. There is no normal health loop to burn down, so emptying a potato chest into the body does not solve the event.

sections.heading: Read the Missile Cycle
paragraphs: The attack sequence uses twelve launch positions. Early shots carry wider target offsets; later cycles tighten the spread. Players are sorted ahead of other character targets, so nearby Wocs do not make a dependable shield.
bullets: Move before the hatch sequence finishes.
Use solid terrain with more than one exit.
Do not stop beside a loaded vehicle or animal pen.

sections.heading: Build for Escape, Not Turret Damage
paragraphs: A compact scout with protected fuel, clear Lift points, and a low center of mass is more useful here than a stationary damage platform. The vehicle should cross uneven ground without trapping the driver in one predictable line.

seo.title: Scrap Mechanic Scannerbot (Seeker Bot) — Missile Survival
seo.description: Use the Scrap Mechanic Scannerbot and Seeker Bot guide to survive the missile sequence, understand normal-attack immunity, and choose a reliable escape build.

name: Blue Totebot
description: A 60 HP water-adapted Totebot that can torpedo through water, switches to 20-damage melee on land, and can drop Circuit Boards, Glue, or a rare Drill.
imageAlt: Official Scrap Mechanic preview showing two Blue Totebots

sections.heading: Get Out of the Torpedo Lane
paragraphs: Blue Totebot is built around a water charge, not the standard Green Totebot chase. Move toward reachable shore at an angle and avoid fighting beside a boat, pump, or submerged storage connection you cannot repair safely.

sections.heading: Do Not Shoot the Immune State
paragraphs: The torpedo attack state is included in its immune-state check. Wait for the charge to finish and re-acquire the target on land or during a normal movement window before spending potatoes.

sections.heading: Its Three Loot Rolls Are Independent
paragraphs: Circuit Board, Glue, and the rare Drill use separate checks. The Drill chance is roughly 4.8%, so it is a bonus rather than a dependable equipment route.

sections.heading: Water Builds Need a Recovery Edge
paragraphs: Place important pumps and chests where the player can reach them from shore. A system that only works while standing in the torpedo lane turns a small bot encounter into a full farm shutdown.

name: Yellow Totebot
description: An 80 HP jumping Totebot that uses stomp attacks across vertical structures, always drops 1–2 Circuit Boards, and can add 3–7 Batteries.
imageAlt: Official Scrap Mechanic preview showing two Yellow Totebots

properties.value: Vertical clearance, not wall height alone

sections.heading: A Low Roof Is Not a Complete Defense
paragraphs: Yellow Totebot was built to jump and stomp through vertical layouts. A farm entrance that stops Green Totebots at ground level can still expose roof-mounted Controllers, Pistons, or crop storage to the landing path.

sections.heading: Wait Out the Immune Movement
paragraphs: Its jump and patrol-related states are included in the damage immunity check. Track the landing and fire during a normal combat window rather than spending shots during the leap.
bullets: Keep valuable mechanisms away from the top edge.
Leave lateral space to exit the stomp area.
Test the gate with an overhead clearance route, not only a ground push.

sections.heading: Reliable Boards, Conditional Batteries
paragraphs: Every normal kill awards one or two Circuit Boards. The second roll gives three to seven Batteries two-thirds of the time, making Yellow Totebot a stronger energy-material encounter than the standard Green Totebot.

sections.heading: Repair the Landing Zone First
paragraphs: After a fight, inspect roof plates, overhead wiring, and the outer edge of moving mechanisms before repairing cosmetic walls. The stomp route can damage a part that still looks connected from ground level.

sections.heading: This Is Not a Farmbot With More Health
paragraphs: Trashbot damage is controlled by the current attack pattern and eye state. Firing continuously at a closed weak point wastes ammunition and blocks your view of the next shockwave or projectile wall.

sections.heading: Thirty Health Is Per Phase, Not the Whole Fight
paragraphs: Both fight configurations use thirty health per phase before multiplayer scaling. The arena records the highest player count it has encountered, so a group fight does not collapse back to a solo health expectation when someone leaves the immediate area.

sections.heading: Five Core Hits Complete the Recovery Window
paragraphs: After the damage phase opens the core opportunity, the fight expects five core hits before recovery. Assign a clean shooting lane instead of stacking every player on the same dodge path.
bullets: Enter with a separate movement lane and firing lane.
Reload before the eye-open window.
Move away from the 30-unit explosion area when the pattern demands it.

sections.heading: Bring a Transport Build, Not a Boss-Fighting Vehicle
paragraphs: Use a scout or hauler to reach the arena and stage supplies, then park outside the projectile space. The encounter is built around player movement and weak-point timing; a large vehicle becomes an obstacle unless the arena specifically calls for it.
